summary: The assessee , a Hindu Un divided Family , was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66 and 1967 67 . In respect of the amounts representing accrued interest on the money lending investments , the Wealth Tax Officer included in his net wealth an amount of Rs . 1 , 50 , 000 estimated as the value of all the assets belonging to the assessee on the valuation date . On appeal by the assessee , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that since no income had accrued from the investment made out of the said investments , it could not be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee . He also rejected the contention of the Revenue that the assessee should have been taxed under section 7 ( 2 ) of the Act . The Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Asstt . Commissioner holding that the capital gains arising from the investments were liable to be included within the net wealth of the asses see . The High Court dismissed the reference filed by the Revenue . Dismis sing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . The principle underlying section 3 of the Wealth tax Act is that every asset which is acquired or available at any time before the 1st day of April , 1957 , must be deemed to belong to the person who has received the asset immediately before that date . [ 310 B ] 2 . It is well settled that when a statute provides that something shall be deemed " to accrue ", then unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context , the words " accruing " and " accrued ". are to be construed according to their plain natural meaning . [ 311 E F ] 3 . The expression " earned " means accrued or receivable . There can be no doubt that whatever may be the source of the receipt of the income , the accrual would be regarded as ' accrued '. But where the asset is an asset other than cash , its value is determined pursuant to sub section ( I ) of section 7 as the estimated price , which , in the opinion of the wealth Tax Officer , the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date . If this is so , then the notional value will be taken into account . [ 312 D G ] 4 . The definition of " net wealth " in section 2 ( m ) of Wealth Tax Act includes " net assets " which consist of cash , securities , deposits , stocks , shares , debentures , bonds , stock , notes , etc ., but does not include divid ends . Therefore , the expression " net Wealth " occurring in section 3 ( 1 )( b ) of Income Tax Act cannot be given a restricted

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Be as Sut le j Link Project , Sundernagar . He was also working in the said place of work . In the year 1969 he was charge sheeted for having committed misconduct under Rule 16 ( 1 )( d ) of the Central Civil Services ( Classification , Control and Appeal ) Rules , 1965 . An enquiry was conducted against him on the ground that he had not been given proper opportunity to defend himself . After considering his reply , the En qu iring Officer found him guilty of the charges levelled against him . On appeal by the respon de nt , the appellate authority set aside the order of punishment imposed upon him and directed reinstatement with full back wages . The appe l l ant challenged the aforesaid order before the Tribunal which upheld the same . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the disciplinary proceedings were initiated against the delinquent employee after his retirement from service , it would be open to the employer to proceed further in accordance with law . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . 1 It is well settled that where an inquiry is held under the relevant rules or regulations governing the conditions of service of employees , the principles of natural justice are required to be followed . [ 11 D E ] 2 . 1 The nature of the power conferred on the competent authority under Regulation 3 ( 4 ) of t he Regulations is very wide and can be exercised only when there is some prima facie case made out against the public servant . But if the departmental proceeding is found to be vitiated on account of any procedural irregularity or other infirmity , the court may interfere . [ 12 G H ; 13 A B ] 2 : 2 . The scope of judicial review in such matters has been considered by this Court time and again . [ 14 C ] 2 .: 2 . 2 In the instant case , the appellant ' s services were terminated because of the non availability of the post . There was no allegation of mala fide against the appellant . The termination order was passed without giving any opportunity to the appellant to defend his case . Therefore , the order was bad in law . [ 15 F G ] 2 .( i ) The impugned order does not suffer from any infirmity so as to warrant interference . [ 17 E ] ( ii ) The order of dismissal dated 31 . 5 . 1984 cannot be sustained . [ 18 G ]

The appellant was the lessee in respect of seven lots of coconut gr ove situated at Car an z alem belonging to respondent No . 1 , who had been dispossessed from the property on the strength of a lease executed by him in favour of the predecessor in interest of respondent No 2 . Respondent No . 2 filed a suit for declaration and injunction against the appellant and his co tenant alleging that he was the lawful tenant of the said property and also sought possession of the same on the ground that he had paid rent upto December , 1967 without his tenancy having been lawfully terminated . The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to be evicted therefrom as he was a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Act . On appeal , the District Judge reversed the decree and held that since the plaintiff had paid a sum of Rs . 36 00 towards arrears of rent due to respondent no . 1 from January 1968 till June 30 , 1969 , it could not be said that he is a trespasser within the meaning of Section 3 ( b ) of the Bombay R ents , Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act , 1947 . In further appeal , however , the High Court took the view that the suit was barred by virtue of section 58 ( 2 ) of Bombay Rent Act , 1958 which provided that nothing contained in any law shall apply to any proceedings pending before any court or other authority immediately before the commencement of this Act . It accordingly set aside the order of eviction passed by the Trial Court and remanded the case to the Trial court with a direction that if such a situation arises what procedure should the court follow in the matter of disposal of the suit . Hence the present appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . 1 The provisions of Order 7 Rule 10 CPC are applicable only to suits instituted after 1st July , 1962 when the plaint has been presented but the period of limitation prescribed therein will not apply where the suit is instituted more than one year after the date of institution of the first suit . [ 10 35 B ] 1 . 2 The expression " cause of action " used in Order 2 Rule 2 ( 3 ) means facts which give rise to a right or liability . If the suit instituted prior to 1st July 1962 becomes time barred because of the fact that the defendant has been dispossessed during the pendency of the proceeding , then the suit would be clearly barred by reason of Article 54 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act . The petitioners are employed by the respondent Corporation as car p enters in Government service . They were paid a sti pend of Rs . 4 , 000 per month for similar work . In addition to this , they also get other benefits like wages payable to their counter parts in regular employ ments . The petitioners claim that they should be treated as industrial workers and , therefore , entitled to equal pay for equal work . The Industrial Tribunal held that the petitioners are not workmen within the meaning of section 2 ( s ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 . It was further held that since the petitioners had been discharging their duties as car penter / car p enter from time to time , it is an " industry " under the Industrial Dispute Act . The Labour Court directed payment of 50 % of the amount claimed by the petitioners towards daily wage employment . The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the petitioner . Hence the appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The expression ' industry ' used in section 2 of the Factories Act has wide connotation and includes any calling or occupation of work which forms part of or is incidental to any business , trade , undertaking or manufacture . [ 669 C ] 2 . The word ' industry ', according to its dictionary meanings means something connected with another , especially one in the nature of a craft , profession , or v ocation . A workman may be said to have direct relation to another in the course of his trade or av ocation but he must be engaged in some kind of work . He must be doing some skilled or unskilled work . If he does not do manual work or manual work , he cannot be said lo be a workman . But where he works on a job , he would be a worker even if he works in a non professional capacity . Therefore , the employees who come into the picture at the stage of recruitment or appointment will not fall within the definition of ' workmen '. [ 670 G H ; 67 1A E ] 3 . The term ' employee ' occurring in section 2A ( i ) of Industrial Disputes ( Amendment ) Act , 1985 is wide enough to include persons employed in any department of the State Government . The words ' directly employed ' in Section 2 ( e ) of that Act mean only those persons who are directly employed by a contractor and not otherwise . The inclusive definition of these terms shows that all persons employed by contractors whether directly or through an agency , are workmen . The definition of workmen in section I 2 ( z ) of ' the Industrial disputes Act , is wide

The appellant was tried for the mur ders of two young girls and a woman alleged to have been committed on November 1 , 1972 in respect of murder of one Mal an . He pleaded not guilty and claimed that he had been falsely implicated by P . W . 1 at the instance of accused 6 . On behalf of the prosecution three witnesses were examined as eye witnesses . P . Ws . 1 and 2 were the appro ver s who deposed that they had seen the deceased committing suicide by hanging herself from her bed with a rope and that she had told them about the incident to him . P W . 3 also supported the evidence of P . w . 1 regarding the extra judicial confession made before him by accused 5 . The trial court convicted all the seven accused under section 302 read with section 34 I . P C . and sentenced each of them to imprisonment for life . In appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence of death imposed upon accused 6 to rigorous imprisonment for 10 years . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , the Court ^ HELD : ( i ) It is well settled that when a case rests upon circumstantial evidence , such evidence must satisfy three tests ; ( a ) the circumstances from which an inference of guilt is sought to be drawn , must be co g ently and firmly established ; ( b ) those circumstances should be of a definite tendency un err ingly pointing towards the guilt of the accused ; and ( c ) the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt . For instance , certain facts may lead to one inference or the other so as to exclude every hypothesis but the one proposed to be proved . In a case resting on circumstantial evidence if the circumstances are fully established and the chain of events is complete then the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt . [ 266 F G ] ( ii ) There is no rule of law that circumstantial evidence must be fully established beyond reasonable doubt . But where it is established that the chain is complete and the infirmity of lacuna in the prosecution cannot be cured by false defence or plea , the accused can claim acquittal . [ 267 A B ] ( iii ) The circumstances from the evidence do not form a complete chain so as not to leave any reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the Accused and the guilt must be left to the jury . [ 268 D E ] ( iv ) The evidence of the appro witness PW l shows that there was enmity between the deceased and the accused persons because of previous disputes over land

The appellant obtained a power of attorney from the test at rix on August 22 , 1945 . On her death she executed an will in favour of Sad agopal achar and his wife Smt . G nan am bal Ammal ( Respondent 1 ) for the purpose of beque ath ing their properties to them under five items out of which item 3 was given to him by the testator . After the death of the test ati or ' s widow , the respondent filed a suit against the appellant claiming that he had been put in possession of all the properties covered by the will and that after his death the said properties were inherited by him as his heirs . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it holding that the will did not confer any title upon the appellant . In appeal to this Court it was contended that : ( i ) the document dated September 14 , 1946 , created only a life interest in certain properties mentioned therein and that the intention of the testator was clear from the recitals contained in the will itself ; ( ii ) even if the document was read as a whole it could be construed as conferring absolute rights on the leg ate es who were entitled to enjoy the property during his lifetime ; and ( iii ) the words " absolutely possessed " used in section 30 of the Indian Succession Act , 1925 clearly showed that the exec utant intended to create a life estate in respect of all these properties except those specified in Schedule I . Dismis sing the appeal , HELD : ( 1 ) It is well settled that where there are two possible constructions of a Will , one pointing to the intention expressed by the deceased in writing , the one which gives rise to the present case must be preferred . [ 10 56 B ] ( 2 ) If the language of the will leads to an absurd ity , the court should adopt that construction which would give effect to the clear intention of testator . Where the words of a document are capable of more than one interpretation , the proper approach is to adopt that meaning which prom otes the object of the grant made by the author of the deed . [ 11 E F ] ( 3 ) The true legal position may be stated thus : A person who has signed the document without looking into the surrounding circumstances can prove the intention and long possession of the property concerned . But where the document is read as containing a clear intention to create an interest in immovable property , such intention cannot be attributed to the exec ut ants . [ 12 H 13 A C ] ( 4 ) The word " possess " means " to possess " with reasonable certainty

The appellants are manufacturers of electrical apparatus and other appliances . They were paying duty on the goods manufactured by them at their factory gate , which was a part of the manufacturing activity carried on in the premises of the appellant company . The dispute between the parties related to the rate of duty payable on the raw material used for the manufacture of electric ally he ated equipment . The Assistant Collector held that the assessee had not produced any evidence to show that they had been using the ar c carbon s as an aid or add iction to the electric power supplied by the appellant . On appeal , the Appellate Collector held against the assessee but allowed the appeal holding that the use of the ar cs is essential in itself and therefore it could be classified under item 4 . In further appeal to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) The entry does not refer to " ancillary or auxiliary ". It refers only to some incidental or auxiliary activities which may be necessary for the production of electricity . [ 10 56 B ] ( 2 ) The expression ' ancillary ' has been defined in section 2 ( h ) of the Act to mean any process involving the use or ad aptation of energy for the purpose of generating energy , including any direct communication to human life from any wind energy plant or animal life and includes all services provided in connection with such activities . The word ' ancillary ', according to its dictionary meaning means something more than mere distribution of energy . Therefore , the word ' accessories ' must be understood in its ordinary sense . [ 11 C E ] ( 3 ) The word access ory is generally used in connection therewith and not merely in relation to the particular type of instrument . If the words are used in a broad sense , they would have to be given their natural meaning . But if the context so requires , there can be no doubt that the words should be read in a restricted sense . The object of the legislature in enacting the law is to enable the State Government to levy tax on every kind of ap pliance used in the industry . This is clear from the fact that the Legislature did not intend to cover within its ambit any ap pliance designed for the use in project ors . The intention of the fram ers of the statute appears to be that these ap pend ages should be used in projects ors and other cin em as . [ 12 D F ; 13 A B ]

The petitioners are lessees of minor minerals in the State of Gujarat . They filed petitions under Article 32 challenging the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26 , 1985 which provided that no royalty shall be charged from Nim bha das of village pot ters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year . The petitioners challenged the vires of section 15 of the Act and contended that the said provision was violative of article 301 of the Constitution inasmuch as it violated the fundamental right guaranteed to them under Articles 19 ( 1 )( g ) and 301 of Constitution . It was also urged that the provisions of Chapter V of the Rules were discriminatory and unreasonable since they had been made applicable only to those areas where mining operations were not permitted by rules framed under the Act . The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 and the object sought to be achieved by the amendment . The power exercised is legislative in character the authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make rules equ i table by necessary implication . No express power need to confer on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the law . [ 416 C ] 2 . In view of the fact that the powers exercised are legislative in nature the authority concerned may be given to persons mentioned in Rule 9 . The appellant was elected as a trustee of the Kumar an Koil in Manj ak oll ai village . He filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to be elected as trustee of an office which fell vacant under section 6 ( 9 ) of Madras Act 1 of 1925 , and for a declaration that the trustees hip of the temple was not hereditary . The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the trustee had no right to hold the office of trustee till his death and therefore the provisions of section 6 were inapplicable . In appeal by special leave it was contended : ( i ) that the expression " successor " occurring in section 6 of the Act means only one who is appointed or nominated ; ( ii ) that even if there are two dis ci ples , one of them must be from the other and so long as the person is not appointed , the power conferred by section 6 would be available to the other . HELD : ( iii ) Section 6 ( 2 ) does not apply to the present case because the appointment of the first respondent as trustee was made after the coming into force of the Hindu Succession Act . [ 428 B ] ( iv ) The word ' succession ' has been defined in section 2 ( 11 ) of the Madras Act I of 1927 to mean any kind of inheritance whether by test ament ary disposition or otherwise . It is well settled that the term ' successor ' is used in the sense of ' heir ' and not ' heir '. If the meaning given to the word ' heir ', namely , ' heirs ' is restricted to the natural heirs of the deceased then also the words ' heirs ', ' heirs of a deceased person ' will have to be construed in their ordinary sense . [ 429 E F ] ( v ) The definition of ' successor ', as contained in section 3 ( 8 ), clearly shows that the legislature intended to include both the heirs of an existing trustee and those who may succeed to the office . The intention of the Legislature could not be said to be to exclude the heirs from the position of the last surviving trustee . The legislature did not intend to make such a distinction between the two classes of persons mentioned in section 4 ( 5 ). The appellant was convicted under section 302 / 34 IPC and sentenced to death . He appealed to the High Court against his conviction , which upheld the sentence of life imprisonment imposed on him by the trial court . In appeal before this Court it was contended that ( 1 ) there is no evidence to connect the accused with the murder ; ( 2 ) the prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased had been murdered by the accused ; ( 3 ) the medical evidence does not support the prosecution case as regards the injuries sustained by the deceased in the course of assault ; ( 4 ) the recovery of blood stained clothes from the place of occurrence itself shows that the same were found at a distance of about 100 ft .; ( 5 ) the presence of human blood on the weapon used for causing injury to the deceased could not be ruled out ; and ( 6 ) the absence of blood stains on the clothes of the deceased clearly indicates that he was responsible for the murder . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) It is difficult to accept that the testimony of PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR . There are no reasons why the statement of PW 1 should not have been believed . [ 712 E ] ( ii ) The High Court did not take into account the fact that the dead body was recovered from the spot where the body was lying after two days of the incident . The post mortem report showed that the death was due to shock and haemor rhage resulting from multiple fract ures . The doctor who conducted the autopsy noted that the cause of death was asphy xia due to thr ott ling . The postmortem notes show that the neck was cong ested and the trac he a showed fracture of both bones of the skull . The vis cer a showed that there was no mark of injury on the neck or part of the body . The opinion of the doctor that the injuries were caused by hard and blunt substance cannot be accepted because the injuries found on the person of the accused were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature . [ 713 G H ] ( iii ) The conduct of the appellant in leaving the house un attended when he went near his brother ' s wife and then going towards the police station would indicate that he must have gone to the police Station immediately after the incident but he did not go to the Police Station immediately thereafter . The conduct also shows that he did nothing to prevent the police from reporting the matter to the higher authorities . [ 714 B C ] ( iv ) The delay in lodging the first information

The appellants were the heirs and legal representatives of Amar chand . They filed a return for the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 claiming that they had been assessed as an agricultural income in respect of their respective shares in the firm , but no notice was served on them under section 22 ( 2 ) of the Income tax Act . The Income tax Officer rejected the claim . On appeal by the assessee , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount received from the estate of Amar Chand constituted a capital receipt within the meaning of section 24 B of the Indian Income tax , 1922 , and therefore it could not be included in the total income of the deceased person . He also held that since the real isations were made after his death , he was liable to pay tax on such amounts . In appeals to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) The words " any sum payable by him " occurring in sub sections ( 4 ) and ( 5 ) of section 23 are wide enough to include all sums which may have been paid by the deceased during his lifetime or towards his share of profits . [ 710 F ] ( 2 )( i ) It is well settled that where a statute provides that a certain sum should be paid out of the assets of a business , there can be no doubt that the said sum would be taxable as income if it was actually received in the previous year . If the legislature intended to treat the sum as income , then the fiction must be given its full effect . But when the Legislature used the expression ' shall ', it did so in order to make the provisions of the Act applicable to the case . [ 711 D E ] ( ii ) The word ' shall ' has been defined in section 3 ( 8 ) of Act 43 of 1948 to mean ' prescribed by rules '. Section 24 B defines ' annual value ' and section 24 C says that the aggregate amount of the expenditure incurred in earning the income of a dealer shall be computed in accordance with the provisions contained in section 6 . Under section 24 A , the tax is levied upon the actual receipts of each year . The question whether the amount is dedu cti ble from the gross income of an assessee depends upon the true nature of the transaction and the circumstances in which it is brought into existence . [ 712 G H ] ( iii ) The scheme of the section shows that the liability to pay income tax arises only once . The petitioners were employed in the Andhra Pradesh State . They were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad . On January 19 , 1969 they were transferred to the former Hyderabad State by order dated February 28 , 1969 . The Government of Andhra Pradesh then passed an order under section 3 ( 2 ) of the Public Employment ( Require ment as to Res idence ) Act , 1957 which provided that " every person who is a member of any service or holds any other office of profit under the Central or State Government shall be appointed by such authority and on such terms and conditions as may be specified in the order ". By another order dated March 21 , 1969 relieving all non domicile persons appointed on or after November 1 , 1956 to certain categories of posts reserved for domic iles of Tel eng ana region with effect from April 1 , 1958 , the Government of India issued orders fixing inter se seniority between the petitioners and the respondents . In pursuance of these orders , the petitioners were promoted to the post of Upper Division Clerks and thereafter to the posts of Lower Division Clerks . The petitioners challenged the validity of the said orders before this Court contending that : ( i ) since the impugned orders were made without giving them reasonable opportunity of being heard , their action was discriminatory ; ( ii ) even if it was held that there was no rational basis for making the impugned promotions , the same could not be sustained because the principles of natural justice had been violated ; ( iii ) the impugned order did not disclose any reason why the petitioners should have been reverted to their substantive posts ; ( iv ) the reasons given by the Government for passing the impugned administrative orders were wholly extraneous and irrelevant ; ( v ) the orders were violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the petitioners had been deprived of their right to livelihood ; ( vi ) the order was bad as it was based on mala fides ; ( vii ) the grounds contained in the impugned notifications were vague and indefinite and therefore the impugned notices were invalid ; ( viii ) the power conferred upon the Government to issue directions to the authorities concerned was arbitrary and unreasonable ; ( ix ) the petitioners ' rights guaranteed under Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution were infringed by the impugned executive orders ; ( x ) the Government acted arbitrarily in issuing the impugned instructions and thereby deprived the petitioners of their livelihood ; and ( xi ) the provisions of the impugned Government Orders were violative Of article 14 of Constitution . The appellant was a trade union official and he was charged with offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act , 1898 . He alleged that on May 12 , 1956 , when the house in which the appellant resided had been searched by the C . I . D ., Inspector , S . N . Singh , the Sub Inspector purported to make a list of articles found in his al mir ah as also those belonging to the father . On enquiry it was revealed that the appellant ' s father had opened an account with the Bank at Delhi and that he had withdrawn from it Rs . 50 , 000 / as advance against the cash credit balance . The appellant denied having opened any such account or opening any current account with him . It was further contended that the entry in the general diary showed that the money belonged to the appellant who used to open the same for some time and that this amount was not shown to have been deposited in the bank but was kept in the joint account of the appellant . Held , that the entries made in the General Diary did not show that the amount of Rs . 10 , 000 /- was deposited in his personal account . There was no evidence to show that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the accused . No presumption can therefore be drawn against the appellant that he must have secre ted them from the mere fact that they were found in the al mir o sh .

The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of contempt of court for disobey ing an order passed by it . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) A person who is not a party before the court cannot be said to have committed contempt of the court because he has not been duly authorised to administer oath s under section 85 of the U . P . Panchayat Raj Act , 1947 . [ 117 B C ] ( 2 ) Section 3 of the Uttar Pradesh Panchayat Raj Adhiniyam , 1947 provides that no suit or other legal proceeding shall lie against any member of the Panchayat in respect of anything done or purporting to be done in good faith under the provisions of the Act and rules made thereunder . It does not make any difference whether such officer had knowledge of the order of the High Court or not . If there is un impeach able evidence that the judicial officer had received information from the office of the panchayat concerned about the filing of the application before him , then the question arises as to what were the facts stated in the application which are relevant to the enquiry . [ 118 D E ; 119 F G ] ( 3 ) There is nothing on record to show that the Sarpanch and the Pan ch as had knowledge about the order when they filed the application . They did not know the existence of the Order of the Ny aya Panchayat nor did they state that the order was placed before them . Therefore , the fact that the Panch as were not well ver sed in law and procedure would not vitiate the proceedings . [ 120 H ]

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 , I . P . C ., and sentenced to death for committing the murder of Sheo Sahai . On appeal by the State , the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to rigorous imprisonment for life . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that ( 1 ) there was no evidence in support of his case that he had committed the murder ; ( 2 ) even if the prosecution story were true , the fact that the deceased was murdered at night or early morning did not make any difference because the occurrence took place at about mid night when the appellant was only a labourer ; ( 3 ) the extra judicial confession made by the appellant to Uj agar Singh could not be relied upon as a dying declaration since the Sub Inspector who recorded the statement had not been examined as a witness ; ( 4 ) the Additional Sessions judge erred in relying on the extra Judicial confession of the accused which was retracted after nearly two years of the incident ; ( 5 ) the Extra Judicial confession is inadmissible in view of section 24 of the Indian Evidence Act , 1872 , inasmuch as it was made before the police officer during investigation and therefore inadmissible in evidence ; and ( 6 ) the evidence relating to motive should have been excluded from consideration . HELD : ( i ) It is well settled that where an alleged confession is made by one person to another with a view to aid the other in order to escape punishment for murder , such confession must be held to be admissible against the co accused unless the court is satisfied that it was obtained by threat or promise having regard to all relevant circumstances including the nature of the offence itself . [ 205 E ] ( ii ) There are several circumstances which show that the appellant ' s conduct in purchasing a sword and delivering it to the Police Officer has influenced the mind of the witnesses and resulted in the commission of the crime . The extra judicial confessional statement of the appe l l ant cannot be rejected merely because it is retracted later . If the extra - judicial confession is found to be voluntary and true , then also the extra j arg um rule regarding admissibility of the extra evidence does not apply . [ 206 F G ] ( iii ) The extra Judicial confessional statement is admissible in evidence provided it is corroborated by other independent evidence . [ 207 B ]

The petitioners , who were elected to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December 1978 and had filed their nominations on November 25 , 1978 for election to the post of Mayor of a Municipality under section 16 ( 1 ) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act 1956 challenged the validity of the elections held on December 28 , 1978 . They also prayed that they should be declared as elected . The Collector of Raipur passed an order dated October 21 , 1978 declaring the result of the election on December 31 , 1978 and directed the Returning Officer to complete the election process within six months from the date of the publication of the said order . On January 11 , 1979 , the Collector issued a notice calling upon the petitioners to attend the office on December 30 , 1978 at 10 . 00 A . M . and to show cause why the election should not be set aside . The petitioners submitted their objections to the aforesaid notice but no orders were passed thereon till December 28 . 1978 . Thereafter , the final publication of electoral roll was done on November 16 , 1978 by the Collector of Bilaspur . The petitioner ' s case was that since the last date for filing nomination papers was April 20 , 1978 , it must have been concluded before that day when the scrutiny of the nomination papers took place . It was contended that the rejection of the petitioners ' objection after the expiry of the time prescribed for filing the petition was arbitrary and illegal inasmuch as there was no compliance with the provisions of Section 33 ( 4 ) of Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act , 1961 which required the Returning officer to fix a date for scrutiny of each nomination paper and to declare the results thereof . The contention was rejected by the Election Tribunal holding that the date fixed for scrutiny could only be the date on which the scrutiny would take place and not the date when the list of contesting candidates was published . In appeal to this Court , HELD : 1 . The High Court has rightly held that the question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dis s enti ents a person to relief under Article 226 of the Constitution can be justified if it finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for the delay in preferring the petition although it may hold that there was an error in the notice issued under Rule 4 ( 1 ). [ 384 B C ] 2 . The power of the High Court under Article 227 of the constitution cannot be exercised so as to upset or reverse the decision rendered by the first respondent . [ 385 E F ] 3 . The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act , 1913 . It had a share capital of Rs . 1 lakh divided into 10 lakhs shares and 8 lakhs shares out of which 2 , 000 were held by the directors in their individual capacity . In respect of this share it was contended that there was no general body meeting as required by section 133 ( 3 ) of the Act . Held : ( i ) Section 134 ( 4 ) of that Act is not applicable to the present case because the general meeting was not called for the purpose of filing the list but only for the purposes of enabling the shareholders to make an application for registration of the balance sheet and profit and loss account . The Company was a public limited company and it had its registered office in Calcutta . It carried on the business of manufacturing , engineering and other allied industries . In 1956 , there were about 60 workmen employed by the Company . On March 31 , 1959 , the Government of India issued an order under section 10 ( 1 ) ( d ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 , which provided that " no employee shall be dismissed or discharged for misconduct except by way of victi mis ation or unfair labour practice ". The Company challenged this order before the Labour Appellate Tribunal , but without success . The Tribunal held that the award did not fall within the definition of ' retrenchment ', as defined in section 2 ( oo )( bb ), and therefore , the provisions of section 25 F of the Act would not apply to the case of the workmen . The Company filed an appeal against this decision before the High Court . The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide whether the contract of service between the Company and its employees stood terminated when they entered into the employment agreement with their employer ; that the finding of the Tribunal that the contract was one of dismissal could not be sustained because the dispute related only to payment of bonus ; that even if the contract covered both the categories of workmen , the Tribunal should have decided the question of reinstatement also ; that since the contract itself contemplated payment of compensation at the rate of three months ' basic wages , the award was bad in law ; and that the view taken by the Tribunal was erroneous . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) The conclusion reached by the High court is correct . [ 678 B ] ( ii ) The Tribunal committed an error of law requiring interference by this Court in deciding the matter . [ 679 C D ] ( iii ) The Award of the tribunal was based on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959 , and in doing so , the tribunal took into account the fact that the wage structure of the Company had been revised from time to time . The claim in this respect was made by the workmen in the Reference . But the Tribunal did not take into consideration the said contention . [ 680 G H ] ( iv ) The finding of fact arrived at by the Industrial Tribunal that there was no comparable industry in the region where the Company was situated , was perverse . The finding that the Company has been making profits over a long period cannot be interfered with unless it is shown that the existing wage structure was inadequate . [ 681 E ]

The appellant Corporation was established under the Life Insurance Corporation Act , 1956 . Under section 19 ( 2 ) of the said Act it is provided that every employee in an establishment shall retire on completion of 58 years of age and at any time thereafter on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof . On January 19 , 1956 the Central Government framed a regulation called the Life Assurance Corporation ( Staff ) Regulations , 1960 which came into force with effect from 1st September , 1956 providing for the vesting of the management of the life insurance business in the Corporation . Regulation 19 ( 1 )( b ) provides that where the number of employees to be employed by the Corporation exceeds one hundred , the services of such employees may be terminated after giving one month ' s notice or pay in lieu therefor if they are not suitable for continuous service . In exercise of this power the Central Govt . made regulations known as " The General Insurance ( Emergency Provisions ) Or di nance , 1956 ". By virtue of these regulations the Corporation was empowered to make regulations regarding the conditions of service of its employees including their terms and conditions of employment . These regulations were published in the Gazette of India on February 20 , 1956 and were effective from April 1 , 1957 . The respondent who had been appointed as a general secretary in the Life insurance Corporation of India continued to serve till he attained the age of 60 years . He challenged the validity of the regulations before the High Court contending that since the regulations did not provide for the continuance of the officers and servants of the Corporation beyond the age prescribed for retirement , the impugned regulations were invalid . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no rational basis for fixing the age limit ; but the High court held that the regulations were valid because they were not arbitrary and unreasonable . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The regulations do not lay down any principle or policy for determining the age . They merely prescribe the minimum age of retirement . [ 223 B ] 2 . If the regulations are silent on any particular point then the question of fixing the maximum age limit would not arise . It cannot be said that the provisions of the Regulations are arbitrary or irrational . [ 224 C D ] 3 . The Regulations do not provide that the age should be fixed at 55 years . There is nothing in the Regulations which requires the fixation of the age at 55 . Therefore , the Regulations must be read together

The appellant , a Chief Minister of Haryana and the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court visited the Session division of Bhiwani on 15 February 1975 . The petitioner was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act , 1913 . On August 31 , 1953 , an order was made by the Central Government under section 5 ( 1 ) of the Act directing that certain sections of the Taxation on Income ( Investigation Commission for Greater Bombay and other areas ) should be transferred to the Investigation Commission in respect of those cases which had been referred to it under sub section ( 4 ) of section 5 of the impugned Act . In pursuance of this direction the petitioner filed petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of section 6 ( 5 ) of Act XXX of 1947 as being discriminatory in character after the coming into force of the Constitution of India . The petition was dismissed by the High court holding that there were no grounds for making any discrimination between persons who had not submitted their statements but had submitted them without obtaining the consent of the Commission . Held : ( i ) Section 6 ( 3 ) of Ordinance No . 2 of 1949 is valid and intra vires because it provides that all proceedings pending before the Commission shall continue from day to day until they are disposed of according to law ; and ( ii ) the procedure prescribed by the impugned Ordinance has been substantially prejudicial to the assessee inasmuch as he could have his case tried together with others at one hearing only if he so desired .

The Federation was formed for the purpose of promoting Indian business in various parts and in furtherance of its objects . It had a large number of branches , including some of its constituent units . In order to promote Indian business it was necessary that the Association should be registered as an association under section 26 ( 1 ) of the Indian Companies Act , 1913 . The Association was registered with the Registrar of Fir ms on January 28 , 1952 . On February 8 , 1953 , the Association filed a petition before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the registration of the Association on the ground that it was not " a commercial establishment ". The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activities carried on by the Association were not " trade or business " within the meaning of section 2 ( 5 ) of Act 18 of 1955 and therefore no part thereof could be said to have been used for any other activity of the association . Dismis sing the appeal , HELD : ( i ) The definition of ' trade or profession ' given in section 2 of the Act is wide enough to include any profession , trade or calling but does not necessarily mean something more than mere skill . [ 351 E ] ( ii ) The expression " trade " has been defined in section 11 of the English Customs and Inland Revenue Act 1885 with reference to the activity of a trading or business activity . Under section 2 sub clause ( d ), " trade ", means any adv enture or concern in the nature of trade or commerce ; and includes a running away from one place to another . Therefore , the word " trade ' must be understood according to its dictionary meaning . [ 352 C D ] ( iii ) The words " trade , business , or profession " are very significant and they indicate that the activity must be analogous to trade or occupation . They do not mean only production or distribution of goods . But there can be no doubt that the concept of " trade and business " cannot be extended to all cases where the activity falls squarely within the ambit of the definition . [ 353 F G ] ( iv ) The fact that the respondent company is a partnership firm is immaterial because the Memorandum of Association itself provides for the constitution of the Board of Directors which would constitute a body corporate having such members as may be appointed by the Government . [ 354 B ]

The appellant , a Hindu undivided family owned certain landed property in the district of Ben aras . In 18 37 there were some disputes between the British Government and the estate holder . The properties belonged to one Raja Chet Singh who was the original f ounder of the estate . He died on July 17 , 18 37 leaving behind his widow Smt . B ina Devi and two sons . On June 7 , 18 38 , the estate devol ved upon him as his heirs . By an agreement dated March 23 , 18 36 executed by the Nawab of Ban aras , the Rul er of Ban sia granted a pension of Rs . 36 , 322 / 8 / to Babu A us an Singh for the year 18 37 . The amount of pension was calculated on the basis of 1 / 4th of the revenue of the Jagir . By this arrangement the revenue or land colle cti ble tax became payable . The quantum of that pension was determined at Rs . 35 , 322 /. The question now arises whether the allowance is revenue income or not . Held , that it is not taxable under section 4 ( 2 ) ( xv ) of the Indian Income tax Act , 1922 . Section 4 ( 3 )( ix ) of that Act provides that if any person dies after having made a will beque ath ing his property therein , then without being liable to be taxed during the lifetime of such exec utant , the value of the property shall be assessed in the manner provided in sub section ( 5 ). Under the terms of the settlement the ann uity was payable only when the death took place before the date of vesting . It could not be said that the payment was made out of compensation money received from the State . The fact that the deceased had no issue but he left behind his wife and children would not make any difference because the grant of pension did not depend on the death of the grant ee . The mere fact that a life interest was created in favour of another heir does not necessarily mean that the character of the payment has been changed into that of a capital receipt . The right to receive the pension accrued to the recipient on the date when the deed of relinquishment was executed . The payment was therefore not in consideration of the creation of the title in the property but merely as a condition of the enjoyment thereof . The liability to pay the pension arose on the termination of the tenure of the service and hence the character which existed at the time of the making of the endowment ceased .

The appellants are entitled to get their present sal a ry re fixed after giving them actual promotion but they cannot claim any financial benefit retrospectively . [ 111 E F ] 3 . 2 The appellants can be granted the same relief which was granted to them in the Writ Petition filed by the Union of India against the order passed by the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Civil Appe l ment No . 440 of 1981 . The appellant State Transport Authority , by its proceedings dated April 30 , 1984 granted three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation . One permit was granted to the Mysore State Transport Undertaking and two permits to it were granted on the basis of applications from the non preferred category having been made for a period of one year each . On an application filed by the respondent , the Regional Transport Authority rejected the grant of these permits holding that there was no justification for granting them . In appeal before the Tribunal , the State Transport Appellate Tribunal held that the grant was not in public interest but only to benefit the private operators who had already obtained permits under the Act . The High Court dismissed the appeals . Hence the appeals by special leave . Allow ing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . The scheme does not prohibit the grant or renewal of any number of permits except with the prior approval of the Central Government . [ 1019 D ] 2 . The object of the proviso is to ensure that the existing stage carriage operator should be able to operate his vehicle as long as he holds a permit issued under the provisions of the Act and the rules framed thereunder . It also aims at maxim ising the use of vehicles which are generally available across the road without causing inconvenience to other travelling public . The provision for giving preference to the existing operators in respect of over all number of vehicles has been designed to serve the national interest . Therefore , if the State transport undertaking wants to give more than 12 % of the total number of buses to the general public , it cannot be said that the State Government would have given the same treatment to the private operator as they would have done if the permit was being granted . [ 1020 E F ] 3 . The power conferred upon the State authorities to grant approval to the Scheme must be exercised reasonably and fairly . The State Transport Authorities have the undou bted power to refuse the grant / renewal of permits to private operators and reduce the number of existing permits to be granted . This power has to be exercised bona fide for the benefit of the public . [ 1022 B ] 5 . The fact that the appellants did not satisfy the conditions imposed by the statute itself shows that their refusal to grant the permits was justified . [ 1023 A ] 6 . The appellant was appointed senior jail or , Sur endranagar District Jail . He filed a petition for leave to appeal under section 60 ( 2 ) of the Act before the High Court against his conviction and sentence . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The High Courts have power to issue writs in appropriate cases where there is an infringement of fundamental right or where the breach of contract is such as makes the enforcement of the right impossible ; but when the court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit , its jurisdiction must be held to be excluded if there is a clear violation of the principles of natural justice . Court from interfering with the discretion of the Government in matters relating to contracts within the meaning of article 311 of the constitution . [ 182 G H ]

The appellant was a cross cut ter and an employee of the respondent . He had been suspended pending inquiry under r . 18 ( a ) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry , and therefore his services were terminated on account of his grave in discipline and misconduct . On June 21 , 1958 , he served a charge sheet upon him alleging that while functioning as a sub contractor he had caused loss to the company by not making payment of wages for some days during the period between July 1 , 1958 and July 2 , 1958 . The management did not take any action against the workman but proceeded with the enquiry after giving him a show cause notice . After considering the evidence adduced before it the tribunal came to the conclusion that there was no reason why the appellant should be retained in service . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that ( i ) the order terminating the services of the workmen was bad because : ( a ), the termination was mala fide ; ( b ) the employer could have taken disciplinary proceedings against the workmen if they were found guilty of misconduct or negligence which would entail punishment ; ( c ) the termination of service was mala fides ; ( d ) the Tribunal failed to consider whether the reasons given by the management were relevant to the discharge of its employees ; and ( e ) the industrial court erred in coming to the finding that the termination amounted to victi mis ation or unfair labour practice . Held , that the Industrial Court was right in taking into consideration the fact that the appellant had acted under the contract of employment and that the employer had acted bona fide and was not mala fide . It is well settled that where one party has acted mala fide and the other party has suffered loss due to the act of the other , it cannot be said that the dismissal was wrongful .

The appellant , a film writer of the theatre in question , was granted a lease for a period of three years from January 1 , 1959 to June 30 , 1954 . On November 27 , 1954 , the receiver s granted a licence to the appellant and on August 19 , 1954 he executed an agreement with the respondent company whereby he agreed to give up possession of the cinema theatre and to exhibit cin emato graph films at his premises . In pursuance of this agreement , the appellant filed suit No . 14 65 of 1963 against the respondent for a declaration that it had no right or authority over the cinema building and its compound and that the consent decree operated as res judicata . The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondent . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The order passed by the Trial Court is not open to challenge either before the Appellate Court or the High court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure . [ 442 E ] ( ii ) The expression " case " is wide enough to include a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 CPC . It includes a civil proceedings and is neither limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action . The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life . The appellant was a member of the scheduled caste . On appeal , the Election Tribunal held that the appellant ' s nomination had been wrongly accepted and that the respondent was not qualified to be elected as a member . In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that ( i ) the disqualification under section 5 ( 1 )( d ) of the Act could only be with reference to a person who bore a sur name ; ( ii ) even if the exclusion was by a test other than a caste group , the order would have made that clear ; and ( iii ) the High Court erred in holding that the inclusion of the appellant did not amount to a disqualification within the meaning of article 171 of the Constitution . HELD : ( i ). It is well settled that where the exclusion is by a community or a group of persons , the law must be interpreted according to its language and no general rule can be laid down that when a particular community or group of people profess es different castes or tribes , the statute should be construed so as to exclude them from being considered as belonging to such communities or groups . If the legislature has chosen any one of these three classes , namely , those castes or groups , it cannot be said that the sub classification is based upon some intelligible differentia having a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved . [ 11 32 B C ] ( iii ). There is nothing in Article 341 or article 342 of the Con sti t ution to show that the President or Governor of a State has been authorised to make rules prescribing qualifications for membership of a caste or tribe or part thereof or group within a caste . The expression " sub classification " used in article 341 means that wherever a caste is mentioned in the Schedule , all castes are deemed to be included therein . Therefore , the word " sub division " occurring in article 342 does not include sub divisions of a tribe . [ 12 33 D ] ( iv ) The words " sub di vide " do not mean that the whole caste is taken out of the purview of article 342 . [ 1234 F ]

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the service of the State Government . The plaintiffs applied for a certificate under Arts . 133 ( 1 )( a ) and 133 ( 2 ) of the Constitution , which was granted by the High Court on October 28 , 1968 . On appeal to this Court it was contended that : ( i ) an order granting interim injunction does not determine the rights and obligations of parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit ; ( ii ) even if there is no final decision as regards the right or obligation of the parties , such an order can be challenged only in proceedings before the court where the original proceeding is pending and not in other proceedings ; ( iii ) since the order refusing to grant interim injunction did not determine any rights or obligations of the party in relation thereto , the application made by the plaintiff was incompetent ; ( iv ) the order granting the certificate had become infructuous because the plaintiff ' s suit itself was disposed of by the trial court ; and ( v ) the decree obtained by the plaintiffs was not exec utable against them . HELD : ( I ) In view of the express provisions contained in article 133 ( l ), the expression " judgment , decree or final order " occurring in article 132 ( 1 ) must mean judgments or orders passed by the Supreme Court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction . They do not in terms refer to judgments or decrees of courts outside India but they may be regarded as judgments or Orders passed in the course of domestic arbitration . If the order rejecting the application for revocation of the certificate is held to be an interlocutory order , then the question whether the applicant has been able to make out a case for interference with the impugned order would arise at all . [ 698 F G ] ( iii ). It is well settled that the power conferred upon the High Courts under Article 226 of the constitution to issue directions is confined to cases involving substantial questions of law . A writ petition challenging the validity of an order of the subordinate tribunal cannot be said to be a proceeding in the nature of a declar atory one . An order granting a certificate can be questioned in a writ petition under article 226 of Constitution if the conditions laid down therein are satisfied . The High Court could not have issued a writ merely because it thought that the point involved was argu able . But the High court should have refused to entertain the writ petition on the ground that it was premature . [

The appellant company was manufacturing cloth and the process or had been selling it to its customers . The price at which the processed fabric would be sold by the appellant company to their customer was Rs . 5 , 000 per 100 bags of grey cloth plus the value of job work done plus profit and expenses . The assessable value of the processed fabrics was determined as under : ( i ) Cost of the grey cloth in the hands of the process ors plus the cost of the job worked out on the basis of the cost incurred by them ; ( ii ) Cost including the labour charges for the processing ; ( iii ) Cost on the packing materials used in the manufacture of the goods ; and ( iv ) Profit earned from the sale of the said goods . In order to give a declaration to the process ee that the raw material should be sold to him , the appellant sent a cheque for an amount of Rs . 1 , 00 , 000 towards the price of the finished product manufactured by it . It is only when the raw materials go into the market that they become marketable . If the trader has sold the raw item manufactured by him , he will have to pay excise duty accordingly . The true test is whether the raw article is capable of being sold in the market without being sold to the purchaser . If it is so , then obviously the manufacturer would get the raw commodity manufactured

The appellants were allotted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3 / 4 units in the village Rai kot . They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the cancellation of their allotment on the ground that these persons were entitled to allotment of sub urban land at all . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no violation of any fundamental right of the appellants , but it held that the provisions of section 19 ( 1 ) of the Act had been violated by the cancellation . In appeal to this Court : HELD : ( i ) Section 19 ( I ) of ' the Act is completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of allotment is concerned . It does not deal with cancellation of allotment in the sense that it permits cancellation only on certain specified grounds and , therefore , it cannot be said that s . 19 ( l ) of Act is totally in conflict or inconsistent with section 10A of the . [ 339 D ] ( ii ) There is nothing wrong in the provision which says that if an allottee has been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard he should be heard before his application for restoration is rejected . If the allottee himself is guilty of some misconduct or other sufficient reason then such an order can be challenged in a writ proceeding . The Public Service Commission had invited applications for re g ard ing the recruitment examination . On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called for interview and on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed . On the basis Of the result thereof , the appellant was declared successful . He challenged the action of the Public Service Com mission by filing a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed . In appeal to this Court it was contended that ( i ) the process of selection is vitiated because there has been violation of principles of natural justice inasmuch as no opportunity of hearing was given to the appellant ; ( ii ) the order of cancellation of the examination suffers from non application of mind inasmuch as the same was passed without affording any opportunity of being heard ; ( iii ) the procedure adopted by the Public Com mission was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not give an opportunity to the selected candidate to defend himself against the charges levelled against him ; and ( iv ) the entire selection process suffered from the vice of arbitrariness . Allow ing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . It is well settled that if a decision is taken without giving an opportunity of personal hearing or show cause notice , the same can be questioned by the unsuccessful candidate . [ 155 D ] 2 . A person whose name appears in the select list does not acquire any indefeasible right to appointment unless he is appointed by following the prescribed procedure . If he is found un suitable for appointment , his appointment cannot be set aside merely on the ground that he was not selected at all . [ 156 E F ] 3 . There is no rule of law that if one is selected , he should be appointed only after due process of law . No doubt , there are certain exceptions to this general rule but they do not apply where the rules permit such selection . But even in those cases where the State Government appoint s a person with less than minimum merit , the State may still insist upon the requirement of prior consultation with the Public Re ject ing Authority while making the selection . [ 157 G H ] 4 . Where the State Public Service Commis sion has decided to cancel the examination and ask for fresh interview , the question whether the State public service Commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process would not have been lost and the public cause would not had been lost , would not arise . [ 158 B C ]

The appellant filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of possession of certain properties belonging to him . The trial court decreed the suit and directed that he be put in possession of the properties attached by the D era , but dismissed his application on the ground that there was no abatement of the appeal even if he had not been impleaded as party under Order 22 , rule 10 . On appeal , the High Court held that the appellant could not be treated as an interested person within the meaning of O . 22 , r . 10 because he was not impleaded as a party to the suit . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that ( 1 ) since the appellant was duly elected as ma h ant of the D ena and its properties and it devol ved upon him , the provisions of section 4 of the Act would apply ; ( 2 ) though the property belonged to the D ora community , the same did not vest in the D ara or its properties , and therefore , the appellant ' s claim should have been allowed . Dismis sing the appeal , HELD : ( i ) The High Court rightly found that the subject matter of the suit devol ved on Shi am Dass who died during the pendency of the civil suit and thereafter substituted the appellant as a person claiming through her legal representatives . [ 491 B ] ( ii ) The right of the heirs of the deceased Mahant to sue survives only when succession is effected . It cannot be said that the estate vests in the heir of the last surviving trustee . If the interest of the successor is not affected then the appellant can maintain an action for setting aside the abatement . [ 492 C E ] ( iii ) The question whether the appellant has any locus standi to file the suit does not arise at all . The appellant being a member of the family of the late Mahant Shri Jagannath Das , she must be deemed to be a necessary party to bring on record the legal representatives of the predecessor in office . [ 493 G H ] ( iv ) The appellant having failed to implead herself as a respondent in the proceedings before the High court , the decree passed by the trial court cannot be set aside merely because she was impleaded as one of the defendants . [ 494 A F ]

It does not violate any fundamental right or other legal right . [ 591 C D ] 3 . The object underlying the provision for amending the Fundamental rules is to provide certain conditions of service for persons serving in connection with the affairs of the Union or States . This object cannot be achieved unless the legislature has indicated its intention to make such provisions retrospective . [ 592 E F ] 4 . In order to determine whether an enactment is reasonable or not , the court must consider all relevant factors including the nature and character of the legislation , its purpose intended to be fulfilled , the remedy sought to be applied to find out what the enactment is , the object of the enactment and the resultant effects which it seeks to attain , the antecedent state of affairs , the prevalent conditions at the time of its enactment , the surrounding circumstances , the mischief intended to he remed ied and the remedy proposed to be remed ied . [ 593 H ; 594 A B ] 5 . The words " nothing in this sub clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes , or prevent the State from enacting at any time any law having effect as if the provisions of the law were in force at the date of commencement of the Act , are sufficiently wide to enable the State Government to make laws retrospectively . [ 595 C D ]. 6 . The expression ' law ' used in entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution includes the law relating to taxes . [ 596 C ] 7 . The appellants are dealers in the State of Haryana . They purchased raw materials for use as raw material in the manufacture of sugar and molasses , which were sold by them to dealers outside the State . In their returns filed under section 9 ( 1 ) they claimed that purchase tax on the raw materials was not payable because the goods had been manufactured out of the raw material purchased from a registered dealer who is liable to pay purchase tax under section 6 of the Act . The assessing authority held that the purchases made by the assessees were sales in the course of inter state trade or commerce and therefore exempt from payment of tax under the provisions of section 24 ( 3 ). On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessments but allowed the appeals and set aside the assessment orders . He also rejected the claim of the assessees for exemption under section 24 sub section ( 3 ) of the C . S . T . Act . A reference was made to the High Court against the decision of the Tribunal . Allow ing the appeals , this Court , HELD : 1 . Section 2 ( e ) of C . T Act defines ' turnover ' as including all sums received by a dealer as consideration for sale of goods . It does not include any sum charged by a manufacturer for anything done by him in respect of the goods returned to him except such sum as may be prescribed . [ 347 B ] 2 . The definition of " turnover " includes both direct and indirect costs and freight charges . The expression " turnover ", in its ordinary sense means the aggregate amount for which goods are bought or sold . The words " turnover during any year " mean the aggregate of the amounts of the sales and purchases incurred within the taxable period after deducting therefrom the actual cost of transportation of the manufactured goods from the place of manufacture . [ 348 E F ] 3 . The word " turnover ' has been defined in section 2 ( p ) of Act 44 of 1976 to mean " the total amount of receipts of a dealer in respect ofthe sales of any goods effected by him during the said year ". The term " turnover includes the aggregate value of the proceeds of sale of the products so sold ". The phrase " turnover in relation to such goods " occurring in section 5 ( 1 )( b ) of Central Sales Tax Act , 1956 would have to be given a wider meaning than what it has in the earlier part of the provision . If the intention of the legislature was to exclude the last portion of the clause , then there was no need to provide separately the first part of that clause and the second part

The appellants were purchasing cas tor oil from the sellers . They claimed exemption under section 10 ( b ) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act , 1953 on the ground that they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and so no tax was real isable on them . Held : ( i ) The words " a person " in section 10 are wide enough to include a registered dealer who is not a registered assessee but a registered firm ; it cannot strictly be said that the declaration has not been carried out by any one who is a registered . owner or dealer as required by section 8 ( b ). Section 10 ( B ) does not require that the certificate should be signed by an authorised officer . It only requires that such certificate must be signed either by the authorised officer or the selling dealer himself . In the present case there was nothing to show that the word " a " was used in the notification dated September 30 , 1956 , which prescribed the manner in which the certificate was to be issued . The use of the word ' a ' indicates that the intention was to levy purchase tax on a person who was not a Registered dealer . The words ' a person ' in section 8 do not necessarily mean a registered manufacturer . The word ' another ' means a person other than a registered importer . The fact that the goods remained the property till the date of the sale would not make the declaration of the intention u seless .

The appellant married the respondent . She was a divorce e under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code , 1973 and she lived with her husband for about 20 years . After the marriage , she started living in England and then went to England where she had been staying at Bombay . In 1956 , she filed an application before the Magistrate under section 127 ( 3 ) Cr . P . C ., praying that the order be made absolute as she did not want to live with him but wanted some reasonable arrangement for meeting expenses during the period when he was away from India . On appeal , the Sessions Judge held that the parties were governed by the Hindu Law ; but the High Court reversed the decision holding that the provisions of section 127 applied only to cases where there is no express provision for payment of maintenance or the amount fixed by customary or personal law has been agreed upon between the parties . This object cannot be achieved unless the legislature intended to do so . [ 83 F G ] 3 . The object of section 125 is social justice which should be given its full meaning and effect . The expression " provide for maintenance " in section 127 must receive a broad interpretation because the scheme of the Act is that the benefit of maintenance should be available to the wife even though she is unable to maintain herself . The appellant was the successful bidder for a sum of Rs . 11 , 900 in respect of his bid amount . He challenged the order dated 25 . 3 . 1988 before the High Court by way of writ petition which was dismissed on 26 . 3 1988 . Thereafter he filed another writ petition challenging the cancellation of the bid and also seeking quashing of the letter dated 25th March , 1988 issued to him by the Collector . The High Court allowed the said writ petition holding that no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing any person in respect thereof . In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing the appellant . It was further contended that the appellant being an ordinary citizen having no right of hearing could not have been deprived of such opportunity merely because he did not file any objection against the order passed by the collector . Allow ing the appeal , this Court , HELD : 1 . The order of the Collector is set aside as being violative of principles of natural justice . [ 779 E ] 2 . The question whether the appellant has a right of being heard or not would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case . If the rules do not expressly provide for the same , they cannot be held to be mandatory . [ 780 A B ] 3 . The power conferred under section 20 ( 4 ) of the Act can be exercised only after following the Rules of natural Justice . [ 781 C D ] 4 . The mere fact that the rules are silent about the manner in which the decision is taken does not mean that the authority concerned should give reasons for its decision . [ 782 F G ] 5 . There is nothing in the rules which requires the reasons to be recorded in writing . They must be communicated to the party affected thereby . The reason for the Rule is that the party who wishes to make representation must express his views before the matter is decided . This is so even if the rules require some communication between the parties . [ 783 H ; 784 A B ]. 6 . The expression " personal hearing " used in sub rule ( 4 )( b ) of Rule 19 of the Bihar State Public Works Contract Service Rules , 1947 means giving of notice at least three clear working days in advance to the person against whom action is proposed to be taken . The appellant , a tenant of the premises in question , was inducted as a tenant by the respondent landlord . He filed an application under section 10 ( 2 )( vi ) of the Bombay R ents , Hotel and Lod ging House Rates Control Act , 1947 for fixation of fair rent on the ground that he required the suit premises bona fide for his own use and occupation . The Rent Controller held that the appellant had failed to prove that there was any agreement between him and the respondent regarding payment of rent at Rs . 150 per month . On appeal , the appellate authority set aside the order of eviction but allowed the claim of the respondent landlords holding that the relationship of landlord and tenant did not exist between them and the appellant . In revision before the High Court it was contended that : ( i ) since the tenancy created by the parties was one of the obligations which were imposed upon the tenants by the statute , the contractual tenancy could be terminated only if the conditions laid down therein are fulfilled ; ( ii ) even though the contract of tenancy is based on the performance of the obligation , the statutory right conferred by the contract would still continue to subsist and the rights of the parties would be governed by the terms of the contract itself ; ( iii ) the provisions of the Rent Control Act do not apply to the present case because the lease deed provided that the lessee would pay the monthly rent after every three years and therefore the termination of the tenancy would not affect the rights or liabilities of the lessor and the tenant ; ( iv ) the notice issued by the appellant terminating the tenancy was invalid inasmuch as the same was contrary to the express provision contained in section 4 of the Act ; and ( v ) the notices served by the respondents were illegal and void being violative of the principles of natural justice . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . Section 4 of The Rent Control Ordinance , 1949 , provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force , no person shall let out any building except with the previous permission in writing of the Controller . [ 571 C ] 2 . It is clear from the language of section 4 that the legislature intended that the protection afforded by section 4 should be confined only to cases where the landlord requires the premises reasonably and bonafide for personal occupation . The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1943 44 . In 1949 , he filed a return of his total income showing nil income and claimed that it should be treated as an agricultural income . He also furnished certain particulars about the amounts paid by him in respect of his business during the relevant previous years . The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 13 ( 2 ) of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act , 18 76 requiring the assessee to show cause why the assessment order should not be made against him . On receipt of the reply from the assessee , the assessing authority passed an order on March 30 , 1955 directing the assessee not to pay any amount due to the Government . The assessee challenged this order before the High Court but without success . The High Court held that the order of assessment was invalid because there had been no proper service of notice upon the assessee and therefore the assessment proceedings were illegal . It further held that since the assessee did not file his returns properly , the assessment could not be said to have been validly made . The question whether the assessment was valid or not was left open . Held , that the procedure prescribed by law for making assessments is one of the modes of assessment and if the assessment is made after the expiry of three years from the end of the accounting year , the period of limitation provided by section 34 would apply .

The Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy ( Amendment ) Act , 1953 was passed by the West Bengal Legislature with retrospective effect from January 1 , 1953 . Section 4 of the Act provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any contract or law for the time being in force a tenant shall be deemed to have purchased from his landlord the land held by him as a th ika tenant on the date immediately preceding the commencement of this Act and every such purchase shall be valid unless it is made within one year from the date on which he took possession of the land under section 3 . On March 18 , 1949 , the appellant filed an application before the Subordinate Judge praying that the ejectment proceedings should not be continued against him . He also prayed that the respondent ' s tenancy may be restored . The Subordinate Judge dismissed the application holding that the suit was barred by limitation . In appeal to the High Court , the High court held that the provisions of section 4 were prospective only and did not affect the rights of the parties . It further held that there was no provision for transfer of pending suits and appeals pending on February 28 , 1949 when the Act came into force . Held , that the view taken by the High Courts was correct . Under section 4 of Act 25 of 1949 , all pre Act suits had to be instituted and decrees obtained after the coming into force of the said Act must be treated as decrees and decrees of courts . There was nothing in the Act of 1949 which affected the operation of section 4A of the Calcutta Thi k Tenancy Act , 1949 . The words " decree or order of a Civil Court " occurring in section 4A ( 2 ) of the Bengal Thi ka Ten ants Protection Act , 1947 , mean a decree or other proceeding relating to the right , title or interest of a person who has been dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law . The expression " decree " in section 4 means a decree passed by a civil court . The word " decree ", therefore , does not include a decree of a civil nature .
